Executive Overview

The Divergent Path: Emissions Growth vs. Renewable Adoption

The global climate landscape in 2026 is defined by a profound and dangerous divergence. On one hand, the world has achieved unprecedented milestones in renewable energy deployment, with clean sources now powering more than one-third of global electricity generation[10][38]. On the other hand, total greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise, reaching record highs that push the planet further away from the safety thresholds established by the Paris Agreement[5]. This section synthesizes the core findings of this report, highlighting the structural disconnect between technological progress in the power sector and the broader inertia of the global economy. It provides a high-level overview of emission trends, per-capita disparities, and the widening implementation gap, while excluding detailed policy mechanics or granular regional case studies which are addressed in subsequent chapters.

Critical Warning

Despite significant renewable growth, current policy trajectories project a 2.8°C warming trajectory by 2100, far exceeding the 1.5°C limit[17][17].

The Emissions Paradox

In 2024, global CO2 emissions reached 38,599 Mt, representing a 69.8% increase since 1990[4][7]. This upward trend persists even as the share of renewables in electricity generation climbed to 33.8% in 2025[11]. The paradox lies in the fact that gains in the power sector are being offset by rising demand in industry, transport, and heating, as well as continued expansion in emerging economies. China alone accounted for a 394.8% increase in emissions over this period, becoming the world’s largest emitter with 12,289 Mt in 2024[5]. Meanwhile, India saw the highest relative growth rate at 452.5%, reflecting its rapid industrialization and energy access expansion.

Conversely, major developed economies have begun to decouple economic growth from emissions. The United States reduced its total emissions by 4.4% since 1990, while the EU-27 achieved a substantial 37.3% reduction[6]. These declines demonstrate that decarbonization is technically feasible, yet they remain insufficient to offset global growth. The net result is a planet that continues to accumulate carbon in the atmosphere at an accelerating rate, with daily emissions averaging 116 million tonnes in 2025.

Equity and Per-Capita Disparities

Aggregate national figures obscure significant inequities in individual carbon footprints. Per-capita analysis reveals that citizens in high-income nations continue to emit at rates vastly higher than the global average. In 2024, the average American emitted 14.20 tons of CO2, more than six times the 2.20 tons emitted by the average Indian[9]. South Korea, despite its smaller geographic size, recorded a per-capita rate of 11.29 tons, placing it among the highest emitters globally[37][37].

These disparities complicate international negotiations, as developing nations argue for their right to expand energy access using affordable fossil fuels, mirroring the historical development path of the West. China’s per-capita emissions of 8.66 tons now exceed those of the EU-27 (5.39 tons), marking a pivotal shift in global responsibility. Addressing this gap requires not only technological transfer but also financial mechanisms that support equitable transition pathways.

The Renewable Transition: Progress and Limits

The electricity sector remains the bright spot in the global climate effort. The share of renewables in global electricity generation rose from 19.1% in 1990 to 33.8% in 2025[11]. The EU-27 leads this transition, with nearly half (47.7%) of its electricity coming from renewable sources. China and the United States have also made significant strides, increasing their shares by 16.6 and 14.7 percentage points respectively.

However, electricity accounts for only a portion of total final energy consumption. Heavy industry, aviation, and shipping remain heavily reliant on fossil fuels. Furthermore, the pace of renewable adoption varies wildly. South Korea, for instance, still derives only 10.4% of its electricity from renewables, a modest increase from 4.0% in 1990. India’s share has remained relatively stagnant, growing by just 1.0 percentage point over three decades, despite its massive overall energy demand growth. These laggards highlight that policy ambition does not always translate into rapid infrastructure change.

Scope of This Report

This report provides a comprehensive analysis of the global climate crisis as of late 2026. It examines the historical trajectory of emissions, the equity implications of per-capita data, and the status of the renewable energy transition. It further evaluates the gap between current policies and the Paris Agreement goals, detailing the specific frameworks employed by major economies such as the United States, European Union, China, and India. A dedicated case study on South Korea illustrates the challenges faced by advanced industrial economies with high energy intensity.

Readers should note that this executive summary focuses on high-level trends and aggregate data. Detailed discussions on specific policy instruments (such as the Inflation Reduction Act or the EU Emissions Trading System), granular sectoral breakdowns, and technical barriers to grid integration are reserved for subsequent sections. The aim here is to establish the factual baseline: the world is building clean energy faster than ever before, but it is burning fossil fuels even faster. Closing this gap is the central challenge of the next decade.

Global Emission Trends and Disparities

Global CO2 Emission Trends (1990–2024)

The trajectory of global carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from 1990 to 2024 reveals a profound structural divergence in the world’s energy systems. While total atmospheric loading has continued to rise, reaching an all-time high of 38,599 Mt in 2024, the underlying dynamics vary drastically across geopolitical blocs. Developed economies, particularly the European Union and the United States, have managed to decouple economic activity from absolute emission growth, whereas emerging industrializers such as China and India have driven the bulk of the global increase. This section analyzes these absolute emission trends, highlighting the shifting center of gravity in global climate responsibility.

The Global Aggregate: A Persistent Upward Trend

Since the baseline year of 1990, global CO2 emissions have increased by 69.8%, rising from 22,732 Mt to 38,599 Mt in 2024. This aggregate figure masks significant regional volatility but underscores a persistent reliance on fossil fuels across the global economy. In 2024 alone, energy-related CO2 emissions increased by 0.8%, hitting a record high of 37.8 Gt CO2[3]. When including emissions from land-use change, such as deforestation exacerbated by El Niño conditions, total CO2 emissions were projected to reach 41.6 billion tonnes[7]. Despite decades of international climate diplomacy, there remains no definitive sign that global fossil fuel emissions have peaked[7].

The Rise of Emerging Industrializers

The most dramatic shift in the global emissions landscape has been the ascendancy of China and India. In 1990, China emitted 2,484 Mt of CO2, representing a modest share of the global total. By 2024, this figure had surged by 394.8% to 12,289 Mt, making China the single largest national emitter by a wide margin. This growth reflects the country’s rapid industrialization and its role as the global manufacturing hub over the past three decades. Similarly, India’s emissions grew by 452.5%, rising from 578 Mt in 1990 to 3,193 Mt in 2024. While India’s absolute contribution remains lower than that of China or the United States, its growth rate is the highest among major economies, driven by expanding energy demand to support a growing population and industrial base.

South Korea presents a distinct case of rapid industrial catch-up. Starting from a relatively low base of 251 Mt in 1990, its emissions more than doubled, increasing by 133.0% to reach 584 Mt in 2024. This trajectory mirrors the nation’s transformation into a high-tech industrial economy, heavily reliant on energy-intensive sectors such as semiconductors, steel, and petrochemicals.

Decarbonization in Advanced Economies

In contrast to emerging markets, advanced economies have demonstrated varying degrees of success in reducing absolute emissions. The EU-27 has achieved the most significant reduction among major blocs, cutting emissions by 37.3% from 3,870 Mt in 1990 to 2,426 Mt in 2024. This decline is attributable to stringent climate policies, the expansion of renewable energy, and the structural shift away from heavy industry. The United States has also reduced its emissions, albeit more modestly, with a 4.4% decrease from 5,132 Mt to 4,904 Mt over the same period. While the US remains the second-largest cumulative emitter historically, its recent trend indicates a gradual decoupling of GDP growth from carbon output, supported by recent policy interventions such as the Inflation Reduction Act.

Key Insight

The divergence in emission trends highlights a fundamental challenge for global climate governance: while developed nations are slowly reducing their absolute footprints, the rapid growth in emerging economies continues to drive the global aggregate upward. Without accelerated decarbonization in Asia, global peak emissions remain elusive.

Implications for Global Targets

The persistence of rising global emissions, despite reductions in some developed regions, complicates the pathway to limiting warming to 1.5°C. The 69.8% increase in global emissions since 1990 underscores the scale of the transition required. As China and India continue to industrialize, their future emission trajectories will disproportionately determine whether global targets are met. The data suggests that current policy frameworks in emerging economies are insufficient to offset the momentum of fossil-fuel-driven growth, necessitating a re-evaluation of international support mechanisms and technology transfer protocols.

Global Emission Trends and Disparities

Per-Capita Emissions Analysis

While absolute emission totals define the scale of the climate challenge, per-capita metrics reveal the profound inequities embedded in the global energy transition. In 2024, the disparity between high-income emitters and developing nations remained stark, reflecting divergent stages of industrialization, energy infrastructure maturity, and consumption patterns.

Key Metric

The global average per-capita CO2 emission stood at 4.89 tons in 2024. This baseline serves as a critical reference point for assessing national contributions relative to population size, highlighting that equity in climate action requires differentiated responsibilities.

The United States maintained its position as the highest per-capita emitter among major economies, recording 13.59 tons per person in 2024[9]. This figure represents approximately three times the global average and more than six times the rate observed in India. Despite modest reductions in total emissions since 1990, the US footprint remains disproportionately large due to high energy intensity in transport, residential heating, and industrial processes. South Korea followed with 11.29 tons per capita, reflecting its heavy reliance on fossil fuels for manufacturing and electricity generation despite rapid economic development.

In contrast, China’s per-capita emissions reached 9.13 tons in 2024, surpassing the EU-27 average of 5.39 tons. This crossover marks a significant structural shift: while China’s total emissions are driven by its massive population and industrial base, its individual carbon footprint has now exceeded that of many European nations. The EU-27, however, has successfully decoupled economic growth from emissions through stringent policy frameworks such as the European Green Deal and the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), achieving a 37.3% reduction in total emissions since 1990 while maintaining robust economic output.

India presents a distinct profile, with per-capita emissions of only 2.20 tons in 2024. This low figure underscores the country’s early stage of industrialization and limited access to high-energy-consuming amenities for a significant portion of its population. While India’s total emissions have grown rapidly (+452.5% since 1990), its per-capita contribution remains well below the global average, raising complex questions about equitable burden-sharing in international climate negotiations.

Addressing this disparity requires not only technological innovation but also financial mechanisms that support low-carbon development pathways in emerging economies without compromising their growth objectives.

The Renewable Energy Transition

Renewables Share in Electricity Generation

The global electricity sector has undergone a structural transformation over the past three decades, driven by the rapid deployment of wind and solar photovoltaic (PV) technologies. In 2025, renewable sources accounted for 33.8% of global electricity generation, marking the first time that clean energy surpassed coal as the dominant source of power worldwide[12]. This milestone reflects a cumulative increase of 14.7 percentage points since 1990, when renewables constituted only 19.1% of the global power mix. The transition, however, has been highly uneven across regions, with advanced economies leading the decarbonization of their grids while emerging markets struggle to balance rising demand with fossil fuel dependence.

Key Metric

In 2025, solar power alone met 75% of the growth in global electricity demand, demonstrating its role as the primary driver of new capacity additions[12].

Regional Divergence in Renewable Adoption

The European Union (EU-27) stands as the global leader in renewable electricity integration. By 2025, the bloc achieved a 47.7% share of renewables in its electricity generation, a substantial rise from 13.4% in 1990. This 34.3 percentage point increase was facilitated by aggressive policy frameworks, including the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) and broader policy frameworks, which incentivized the phase-out of coal and the expansion of wind and solar infrastructure. Countries such as Denmark, Portugal, and Spain have exceeded 50% renewable generation, with Denmark reaching 92% in 2025 due to its extensive offshore wind capacity[13].

In contrast, the United States reached a 25.6% renewable share in 2025, up from 10.9% in 1990. While this 14.7 percentage point gain mirrors the global average, the US trajectory has been shaped by state-level mandates and federal tax credits, particularly those expanded under the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA). Solar and wind generation in the US increased seven-fold since 2010, with solar becoming the fastest-growing electricity source. However, the persistence of natural gas as a baseload provider has limited the overall displacement of fossil fuels compared to the EU.

China’s renewable share grew to 37.0% in 2025, an increase of 16.6 percentage points from 20.4% in 1990. As the world’s largest installer of solar and wind capacity, 741 GW of renewable power capacity was added globally in 2024, a significant portion of which was domestic[14]. Despite this progress, China’s total electricity demand has grown so rapidly that fossil fuels, particularly coal, continue to play a major role in meeting baseline load. India, meanwhile, saw its renewable share rise modestly from 23.1% in 1990 to 24.1% in 2025, a mere 1.0 percentage point increase. Although India has set ambitious targets under its Panchamrit Strategy, the sheer scale of its growing energy demand has necessitated continued reliance on coal, limiting the proportional growth of renewables in the power mix.

South Korea remains a notable laggard in the renewable transition. Its renewable share in electricity generation stood at just 10.4% in 2025, up from 4.0% in 1990[13]. This 6.4 percentage point increase is the smallest among major economies, reflecting structural barriers such as grid rigidity, regulatory hurdles, and a historical dependence on nuclear and coal power. While South Korea has implemented the Korea Emissions Trading Scheme (K-ETS), the slow pace of renewable adoption has contributed to its high per-capita emissions of 11.29 tons in 2024.

Structural Drivers and Barriers

The disparity in renewable shares is not merely a function of resource availability but of policy coherence and grid infrastructure. In the EU, the integration of cross-border interconnectors and market mechanisms has allowed for the efficient distribution of variable renewable energy. In the US, the fragmentation of grid management across regional transmission organizations has created bottlenecks, although federal incentives are beginning to address these gaps.

In Asia, the challenge is compounded by the rate of demand growth. China’s ability to scale manufacturing has lowered the global cost of solar panels, benefiting all markets, but its own grid has struggled with curtailment issues during periods of low demand. India faces similar grid constraints, where the lack of flexible storage and transmission infrastructure limits the integration of intermittent sources. South Korea’s low renewable share is further exacerbated by a centralized grid model that prioritizes stability over flexibility, resulting in significant curtailment of renewable output when supply exceeds immediate demand[40].

Leader: EU-27

47.7% Renewable Share (2025)

Driven by policy frameworks, the EU has successfully decoupled economic growth from emissions. Wind and solar now provide the majority of new capacity, with hydropower remaining a stable baseload contributor.

Laggard: South Korea

10.4% Renewable Share (2025)

Despite high technological capability, South Korea’s renewable transition is hindered by regulatory inertia and grid rigidity. The country remains heavily dependent on nuclear and coal, with renewables playing a marginal role in the power mix.

The data indicates that while the global trend is positive, the pace of change is insufficient to meet the 1.5°C target of the Paris Agreement without accelerated policy intervention. The next phase of the transition will require not just capacity addition, but also significant investment in grid modernization, storage solutions, and market reforms to accommodate higher shares of variable renewable energy.

Climate Targets and Implementation Gaps

Gap to Paris Agreement Goals

The discrepancy between current policy trajectories and the Paris Agreement’s long-term temperature goals has widened into a structural implementation gap. Despite the adoption of Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) by nearly every nation, aggregate greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise rather than decline at the rate required to limit global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels[16]. Current policies place the world on a trajectory toward approximately 2.8°C of warming by 2100, a level of heating that would trigger irreversible ecological tipping points and severe socioeconomic disruptions[17][17].

Temperature Trajectory

When the Paris Agreement was signed in December 2015, projections estimated the 1.5°C threshold would be reached by March 2045. As of late 2025, accelerated warming trends suggest this benchmark will be breached by May 2029—fifteen years and ten months earlier than initially anticipated[19].

The Emissions Gap and Policy Inadequacy

The core of the implementation gap lies in the difference between pledged reductions and actual policy enforcement. While many major economies have announced net-zero targets for mid-century, their short-to-medium-term NDCs remain insufficient. The United Nations Environment Programme’s Emissions Gap Report 2025 highlights that nations remain far from meeting the agreement’s goal to limit warming to well below 2°C, let alone pursuing efforts to stay below 1.5°C[16]. Both current policy and pledge trajectories lie well above the emissions pathways consistent with the Paris Agreement’s long-term temperature goals[18].

This divergence is not merely a matter of ambition but of execution. The gap between what countries have promised and what their existing laws and regulations deliver continues to expand. For instance, while the European Union has implemented rigorous mechanisms such as the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) to prevent carbon leakage, other major emitters lack equivalent enforcement structures. The result is a fragmented global response where incremental progress in some regions is offset by rapid industrial expansion in others.

The Inevitability of Temporary Overshoot

Given the current momentum of global emissions, which reached 38,599 Mt in 2024, a temporary overshoot of the 1.5°C threshold is now considered inevitable by climate scientists[15]. Recent analyses indicate that the Earth is most likely to experience a year above 1.5°C sooner than expected, signaling a breach of the Paris Agreement threshold even if long-term averages are eventually stabilized[15]. This overshoot presents profound risks, as crossing critical thermal thresholds can activate feedback loops—such as permafrost thawing and reduced albedo from ice loss—that make returning to safer temperature levels exponentially more difficult.

The concept of "overshoot" implies that global temperatures may exceed 1.5°C for a period before declining later in the century due to aggressive negative emissions technologies. However, reliance on future carbon removal capabilities is a high-risk strategy. The technical feasibility and scalability of methods such as Direct Air Capture (DAC) remain unproven at the gigaton scale required to reverse an overshoot. Consequently, the primary focus must remain on immediate, deep decarbonization to minimize the magnitude and duration of any temperature exceedance.

Figure: Projected global temperature rise under current policies versus the 1.5°C pathway. Data illustrates the accelerating divergence and the likely breach of the 1.5°C threshold by 2029[19].

Required Reductions and Implementation Score

To align with the 1.5°C goal, global greenhouse gas emissions must peak immediately and decline by approximately 43% by 2030 compared to 2019 levels. Current trajectories show no such peak; instead, emissions in major developing economies continue to climb. China, now the world’s largest emitter at 12,289 Mt in 2024, has committed to peaking before 2030, but its annual emissions growth remains substantial. Similarly, India’s emissions rose by 452.5% between 1990 and 2024, reflecting its developmental needs but complicating global mitigation efforts.

The implementation gap is further exacerbated by the slow phase-out of fossil fuel subsidies and the persistent lock-in of carbon-intensive infrastructure. While renewable energy shares have grown—reaching a share globally in electricity generation—this progress is uneven. The EU-27 has achieved a renewable share, but other regions lag significantly, with South Korea and India at 24.1%. Without a synchronized global effort to accelerate the transition away from coal, oil, and gas, the window to prevent catastrophic warming will close permanently.

Addressing this gap requires more than revised NDCs; it demands immediate, binding domestic legislation in all major economies. The next chapter examines how specific policy frameworks in the United States, European Union, China, and India are attempting to bridge this divide, revealing a complex landscape of competitive subsidies, regulatory mandates, and strategic industrial planning.

Policy Frameworks in Major Economies

Policy Analysis: United States & European Union

The divergence in global carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions between major economies is largely attributable to the distinct policy architectures adopted by the United States and the European Union. While both jurisdictions have committed to deep decarbonization, their mechanisms for achieving these goals reflect fundamentally different economic philosophies and regulatory traditions. The United States has pivoted toward a subsidy-driven model centered on the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), whereas the European Union has doubled down on a comprehensive regulatory framework anchored by the European Green Deal and the Fit for 55 package. These frameworks not only dictate domestic emission trajectories but also reshape global trade dynamics through border adjustments and supply chain mandates.

United States

Inflation Reduction Act (IRA)

Enacted in 2022, the IRA represents the most significant climate legislation in U.S. history, deploying nearly $370 billion in energy security and clean energy investments. Unlike traditional cap-and-trade systems, the IRA relies primarily on tax credits to lower the cost of clean technologies.

  • Mechanism: Investment Tax Credit (ITC) and Production Tax Credit (PTC) extended through at least 2025.[21]
  • Target: Reduce U.S. greenhouse gas emissions by 40% below 2005 levels by 2030.
  • Impact: Cumulative global economic benefits from reduced pollution estimated at over $5 trillion from present to 2050.[20]
European Union

Green Deal & Fit for 55

The European Green Deal, approved in 2020, sets the overarching strategy for climate neutrality by 2050.[26] The Fit for 55 package, comprising approximately 19–20 legislative measures, operationalizes the interim target of reducing net emissions by at least 55% by 2030 compared to 1990 levels.[25]

  • Mechanism: Carbon pricing via the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) and regulatory standards.[24]
  • Target: 55% reduction in net emissions by 2030; climate neutrality by 2050.[26]
  • Impact: Expansion of carbon pricing to building and road transport fuels via ETS2, effective 2027.[26]

United States: Subsidy-Driven Decarbonization

The Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) marks a decisive shift in American climate policy from punitive carbon pricing to incentivized deployment. By offering long-term tax credits for renewable energy production and investment, the IRA aims to correct market failures through direct financial support rather than regulatory mandates. The Investment Tax Credit (ITC) and Production Tax Credit (PTC) allow taxpayers to deduct a percentage of the cost of renewable energy systems or receive credits based on energy output.[21] These provisions are designed to accelerate the deployment of clean electricity resources, which is critical given that the power sector remains the largest source of U.S. emissions.

The economic rationale behind the IRA extends beyond domestic emission reductions. Projections indicate that the act will yield cumulative global economic benefits exceeding $5 trillion from the present to 2050, driven primarily by avoided climate damages.[20] Furthermore, the IRA addresses local air quality issues, with lower-bound estimates suggesting health and productivity gains ranging from $20 billion to $49 billion in 2030 alone.[20] This dual benefit structure—global climate mitigation and local public health improvement—strengthens the political viability of the legislation. However, the reliance on tax credits means that the pace of decarbonization is contingent on private sector uptake and the stability of federal funding, which has faced political scrutiny since its enactment.

Investment flows following the IRA’s implementation demonstrate its immediate impact on cleantech sectors. Foreign investment in U.S. cleantech rose from $4.5 billion in the fourth quarter of 2022 to $13.5 billion in the second quarter of 2024, with batteries receiving over 68% of this capital.[23] Imports of key clean technologies also surged, with electric vehicle imports growing from around $5 billion in 2021 to almost $23 billion in 2024.[23] This influx of capital underscores the IRA’s role in reshaping global supply chains, drawing manufacturing capacity to the United States through localized incentives.

European Union: Regulatory Comprehensive Approach

In contrast to the U.S. subsidy model, the European Union employs a regulatory framework that integrates carbon pricing, efficiency standards, and border adjustments. The cornerstone of this approach is the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), the world’s first major carbon market. The Fit for 55 package strengthens the EU ETS by reducing the cap on emissions more rapidly and expanding its scope to include maritime transport.[25] Additionally, the new ETS2, scheduled to enter into force in 2027, will impose a carbon price on fuels used in buildings and road transport for the first time.[26] This expansion ensures that all major emitting sectors contribute to the 55% reduction target by 2030.

A distinctive feature of the EU’s policy framework is the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). Designed to prevent carbon leakage—the relocation of production to countries with weaker climate policies—CBAM imposes a carbon price on imports of certain goods such as cement, iron, steel, aluminum, fertilizers, and electricity.[24] By aligning the carbon cost of imports with that of domestic producers, CBAM protects the integrity of the EU’s internal carbon price while encouraging trading partners to adopt stricter emission standards. This mechanism represents a significant evolution in international climate governance, linking trade policy directly to environmental objectives.

The Fit for 55 package also includes stringent sectoral regulations, such as the Renewable Energy Directive and the Energy Efficiency Directive, which mandate specific shares of renewable energy and improvements in energy consumption.[25] These directives are complemented by the Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation (AFIR), which requires member states to deploy charging and refueling infrastructure for zero-emission vehicles.[24] The comprehensive nature of these measures ensures that decarbonization is embedded across all aspects of the EU economy, from industrial production to residential heating. However, the complexity of implementing 19–20 legislative acts across 27 member states poses significant administrative challenges, requiring robust coordination and enforcement mechanisms.

Policy Divergence

While the U.S. IRA focuses on lowering the cost of clean technology through subsidies, the EU’s Fit for 55 package raises the cost of carbon through pricing and regulation. Both approaches aim to achieve similar emission reduction targets, but they differ in their distributional impacts and political sustainability. The U.S. model relies on fiscal expenditure and private investment, whereas the EU model relies on regulatory compliance and market mechanisms.

Comparative Implications for Global Trade

The juxtaposition of the IRA and the Green Deal has profound implications for global trade and investment. The IRA’s local content requirements have drawn criticism from international partners, including the EU, who argue that they discriminate against foreign producers. In response, the EU has accelerated its own industrial policy initiatives to maintain competitiveness in cleantech manufacturing. Meanwhile, the CBAM introduces a new layer of complexity for exporters to the EU, requiring them to account for the carbon intensity of their production processes. This regulatory divergence creates a fragmented global landscape where companies must navigate differing compliance regimes and incentive structures.

Despite these differences, both frameworks share a common objective: accelerating the transition to a low-carbon economy. The U.S. has seen its per-capita CO2 emissions remain high at 14.20 tons in 2024, while the EU-27 has successfully reduced its total emissions by 37.3% since 1990.[5] The effectiveness of these policies will ultimately be measured by their ability to close the gap to the Paris Agreement goals, a challenge that requires not only domestic action but also international cooperation. As the world’s two largest advanced economies, the policy choices made in Washington and Brussels will continue to set the tone for global climate action in the coming decades.

Policy Frameworks in Major Economies

China and India

The climate strategies of China and India represent the most significant variables in the global effort to limit warming to 1.5°C. Together, these two nations account for a substantial share of current global emissions and future energy demand. China’s emissions reached 12,289 Mt in 2024, while India’s stood at 3,193 Mt, reflecting their rapid industrialization and growing populations. Unlike the United States and the European Union, which have already peaked and reduced their emissions, China and India are still navigating the complex transition from fossil-fuel-dependent growth to low-carbon development. Their policy frameworks are defined by a dual imperative: securing energy reliability for economic expansion while simultaneously deploying renewable infrastructure at an unprecedented scale.

China

Dual Carbon Goals

China officially announced its "Dual Carbon Goals" to peak carbon emissions before 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality by 2060[28][29]. This framework serves as the overarching directive for all sectoral policies, driving massive investments in clean energy technologies.

  • Peak CO2 emissions before 2030
  • Achieve carbon neutrality by 2060
  • Record 430 GW of wind and solar capacity added in 2025[27]
  • Total wind and solar capacity reached 1,840 GW by end-2025[27]
India

Panchamrit Strategy

At COP26, India unveiled the Panchamrit ("five nectars") strategy, a comprehensive roadmap targeting net zero emissions by 2070[33]. The plan emphasizes non-fossil fuel capacity expansion and improved energy intensity without compromising developmental needs.

  • 500 GW non-fossil fuel capacity by 2030[33]
  • 50% electricity from renewables by 2030[33]
  • Reduce carbon intensity of GDP by 45% by 2030[33]
  • Net zero emissions target set for 2070[33]

China: Structural Tension Between Clean Energy and Fossil Expansion

China’s energy transition is characterized by a paradoxical simultaneous expansion of both renewable and fossil fuel infrastructure. In 2025, China added a record 430 GW of wind and solar capacity, raising its total renewable capacity to 1,840 GW[27]. This deployment has been so rapid that some analysts suggest China’s CO2 emissions may have peaked in 2025, following a flat or declining trend from March 2024 through year-end[27]. The clean energy economy, including solar power, batteries, and electric vehicles (EVs), drove more than one-third of total economic growth in 2025 and accounted for over 90% of the net increase in investment[27].

However, this progress is offset by continued coal expansion. By the end of 2025, 291 GW of coal capacity remained in the pipeline, creating a structural tension between decarbonization goals and energy security priorities[27]. Although coal demand in the power sector is declining, the existence of this pipeline increases the risk of carbon lock-in and stranded assets. Deep electrification is advancing, with electricity’s share of final energy consumption increasing from 23% in 2015 to 30% in 2025[27]. Electrification-driven fossil fuel displacement has been concentrated in industry and transport, which together accounted for 85% of the total displacement, with EVs alone contributing 16%[27].

Risk Alert

Despite the decline in CO2 emissions in 2025, Q1 2026 saw a slight 2% rise due to increased wind and solar curtailment, highlighting grid integration challenges[27].

India: Balancing Development and Decarbonization

India’s approach is framed by the Panchamrit strategy, which sets ambitious targets for 2030 while acknowledging the country’s right to develop. The plan aims to achieve 500 GW of non-fossil fuel energy capacity and meet 50% of energy requirements from renewable sources by 2030[33]. Additionally, India committed to reducing its total projected carbon emissions by 1 billion tons and lowering the carbon intensity of its GDP by 45% by 2030. The long-term goal is net zero emissions by 2070[33].

Implementation of these goals has accelerated significantly. In 2025, India added a record 44.5 GW of renewable energy capacity (through November), nearly doubling its annual additions[30]. Investment patterns reflect this shift, with the IEA’s World Energy Investment 2025 report noting that 83% of Indian power-sector investment in 2024 went to clean energy, with solar accounting for the majority[31]. Despite this progress, India’s renewables share in electricity generation has seen minimal growth since 1990, rising only from 23.1% to 24.1% by 2025, a change of just 1.0 percentage points. This stagnation contrasts sharply with the aggressive capacity addition targets, suggesting that overall electricity demand growth is outpacing renewable deployment.

Indicator China India
2024 Total CO2 Emissions 12,289 Mt 3,193 Mt
2024 Per-Capita Emissions 8.66 tons 2.20 tons
2025 Renewables Share 37.0% 24.1%
Primary Policy Framework Dual Carbon Goals Panchamrit Strategy
Net Zero Target 2060 2070

The divergence between China and India is evident in their per-capita emissions and renewable trajectories. China’s per-capita emissions of 8.66 tons in 2024 exceed the global average of 4.73 tons and are approaching those of the EU-27 (5.39 tons)[9]. In contrast, India’s per-capita emissions remain low at 2.20 tons, reflecting its earlier stage of industrial development[9]. China’s renewables share in electricity generation has grown substantially, reaching 37.0% in 2025, up from 20.4% in 1990. India’s share, however, has remained relatively static, indicating that new renewable capacity is primarily meeting new demand rather than displacing existing fossil fuel generation.

Both nations face the challenge of integrating variable renewable energy into their grids. China’s experience with curtailment in early 2026 serves as a warning for India as it scales up its solar and wind capacity. The success of the Dual Carbon Goals and the Panchamrit Strategy will depend not only on capacity installation but on the modernization of grid infrastructure and the implementation of market mechanisms that value flexibility and storage. As the world’s largest developing economies, their policy choices will determine whether global emissions can peak and decline within the next decade.

Case Study: South Korea

Challenges for South Korea

South Korea presents a distinct paradox in the global energy transition. As one of the world’s largest economies and a major exporter of advanced technology, it maintains an emissions profile that diverges sharply from its peers in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). In 2024, South Korea emitted 584 million tonnes (Mt) of carbon dioxide, representing a 133.0% increase since 1990[37]. This growth rate is among the highest in the industrialized world, driven by rapid industrialization and a heavy reliance on fossil fuels for both power generation and manufacturing. While total global emissions rose by 69.8% over the same period, South Korea’s trajectory reflects a structural dependence on energy-intensive industries such as steel, petrochemicals, and semiconductors, which have expanded without a commensurate decarbonization of the underlying energy supply.

The intensity of this challenge is most visible in per-capita metrics. In 2024, the average South Korean emitted 11.29 tons of CO2, a figure that places the country second only to the United States (14.20 tons) among major economies and more than double the global average of 4.73 tons[37]. This high per-capita footprint persists despite significant investments in energy efficiency and the gradual phase-out of older coal facilities. The disparity between South Korea’s economic status and its carbon intensity highlights a critical implementation gap: while national targets align with global climate ambitions, the domestic infrastructure and policy mechanisms required to achieve them remain underdeveloped.

Metric South Korea Global Context
Per-Capita CO2 11.29 tons 2.4x World Avg
Renewable Share (2025) 10.4% Below Global Avg (33.8%)
Emission Change (1990-2024) +133.0% High Growth

Slow Renewable Adoption and Grid Rigidity

A primary bottleneck in South Korea’s transition is the sluggish adoption of renewable energy. In 2025, renewables accounted for only 10.4% of electricity generation, a mere 6.4 percentage point increase from 4.0% in 1990. This stands in stark contrast to the European Union (47.7%), China (37.0%), and even the global average (33.8%). The slow progress is not merely a result of resource scarcity but of systemic grid rigidity and outdated regulatory frameworks. The national target of installing 100 gigawatts (GW) of renewable capacity by 2030 is currently in jeopardy due to a "first-come, first-served" grid connection system that fails to prioritize projects based on readiness or strategic value[42].

This regulatory lag has led to severe inefficiencies. Viable solar and wind projects face prolonged delays while scarce grid capacity remains occupied by fossil fuel plants and non-viable "zombie" projects that have secured connection rights but never commenced construction. The consequences of this misalignment are evident in rising curtailment rates. Between 2023 and 2025, renewable energy curtailment in South Korea increased more than 150-fold, indicating that the grid is increasingly unable to absorb clean energy even when it is available. This waste of clean energy underscores a critical disconnect between generation targets and transmission infrastructure planning.

Critical Insight

Curtailment Crisis: The 150-fold increase in renewable curtailment from 2023 to 2025 signals that grid congestion, not just generation capacity, is now the primary barrier to decarbonization. Without prioritizing "ready and needed" projects, additional renewable installations may simply add to wasted capacity rather than reducing emissions.

Weaknesses in the Korea Emissions Trading Scheme (K-ETS)

The Korea Emissions Trading Scheme (K-ETS), launched in 2015, covers approximately 73% of the nation’s greenhouse gas emissions and serves as the cornerstone of its market-based climate policy[35]. However, the scheme’s effectiveness has been significantly undermined by persistent industry pressure and generous free allocations to high-emitting sectors. In 2025, the carbon price in the K-ETS hovered between USD 6 and USD 7 per ton of CO2, a level far below the estimates provided by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) for achieving meaningful emission reductions[39].

Analysis of corporate climate policy engagement reveals that major industrial actors, particularly in the steel sector and cross-sector associations like the Korea Chamber of Commerce and Industry (KCCI), have consistently advocated for weaker offset rules and higher carryover limits since 2010[39]. This behind-the-scenes lobbying has resulted in a carbon market that provides insufficient financial incentive for deep decarbonization. While companies publicly support South Korea’s 2050 Carbon Neutrality Target, their policy engagement has actively shaped the K-ETS in ways that reduce its ambition, allowing high-emitting industries to maintain business-as-usual operations with minimal cost penalty.

Furthermore, the integration of project-based carbon credits into the K-ETS has introduced complexities that risk diluting the integrity of domestic emission reductions. While the government has established a framework for international mitigation activities under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, aiming to contribute 37.5 million metric tons of carbon reduction by 2030 through overseas projects, the domestic offset regime remains vulnerable to concerns about additionality and permanence[34]. Without stricter oversight and a higher carbon price floor, the K-ETS is unlikely to drive the technological transformation required to meet South Korea’s nationally determined contributions (NDCs).

Structural Impediments to Transition

Beyond policy and grid issues, South Korea faces deep-seated structural barriers rooted in its industrial geography and energy security concerns. The country’s heavy reliance on imported fossil fuels has historically prioritized energy security and cost stability over environmental considerations, leading to a locked-in infrastructure of coal and liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminals. Transitioning away from these assets requires not only new investment but also the managed retirement of existing capital, a process complicated by regional economic dependencies. Coal-dependent regions such as Chungcheongnam-do face significant social and economic challenges as power plants phase out, yet the rollout of renewable energy in these areas is stalled by the very grid connection bottlenecks that plague the national system[42].

Addressing these challenges requires a fundamental reorientation of energy policy. Reforming the grid connection queue to prioritize projects based on development readiness and sustainability criteria is an urgent necessity. Similarly, strengthening the K-ETS by reducing free allocations and establishing a credible carbon price floor would align market incentives with national climate goals. Without these structural reforms, South Korea risks falling further behind in the global race to decarbonize, jeopardizing both its international commitments and its long-term economic competitiveness in a low-carbon world.

Systemic Barriers

Structural Barriers to Transition

The global energy transition faces profound structural impediments that extend beyond political will or technological availability. While renewable energy capacity has expanded significantly, reaching a 33.8% share of global electricity generation as of 2024, systemic barriers rooted in fossil fuel lock-in, grid rigidity, and financial constraints continue to hinder the pace of decarbonization. These structural challenges create a self-reinforcing cycle that delays peak emissions and sustains higher warming trajectories, despite ambitious national targets.

Critical Insight

Fossil fuel infrastructure creates long-term commitment effects. Once capital is invested in coal, oil, or gas assets, economic incentives favor their continued operation to recover costs, creating a "lock-in" effect that resists rapid phase-out even when cleaner alternatives become available.

Fossil Fuel Lock-In and Infrastructure Inertia

The concept of fossil fuel lock-in describes the phenomenon where existing infrastructure and institutional arrangements create high switching costs for transitioning to low-carbon systems. This inertia is not merely technical but deeply embedded in economic models, regulatory frameworks, and supply chains. The continued investment in fossil fuel assets, particularly in developing economies, perpetuates this cycle. For instance, China’s CO2 emissions increased significantly from 1990 to 2024, driven largely by industrial expansion fueled by coal-fired power plants that have operational lifespans of several decades.[5]

This lock-in effect is exacerbated by the merit-order effect in electricity markets, where variable renewable energy (VRE) sources with near-zero marginal costs displace more expensive fossil fuel generators during periods of high availability. However, as VRE penetration increases, the value of each additional unit of renewable energy declines due to cannibalization effects, where renewables compete with themselves during peak production hours.[2] This dynamic can discourage further investment in renewables without adequate market reforms or storage solutions, thereby slowing the transition.

Grid Rigidity and Curtailment Challenges

Electricity grids designed for centralized, dispatchable fossil fuel generation struggle to accommodate the variability and decentralization of renewable energy sources. Grid rigidity manifests as an inability to flexibly adjust supply and demand in real-time, leading to significant curtailment of renewable energy. Curtailment occurs when grid operators must reduce renewable output to maintain stability, effectively wasting clean energy that has already been generated.

Recent data from India highlights the severity of this issue. In 2025, India lost 2.3 terawatt-hours (TWh) of solar generation due to grid security concerns, largely concentrated in the second half of the year.[32] This curtailment occurred because the National Load Dispatch Centre could not reduce other generation sources, such as coal, sufficiently to accommodate midday solar peaks, especially when demand was lower than forecast due to mild temperatures. The total recorded curtailment represented approximately 18% of the average monthly solar generation, underscoring the urgent need for grid flexibility to grow at pace with solar capacity additions.

Similarly, South Korea has faced escalating curtailment issues as it attempts to integrate more renewable energy. Regional output curtailment in the Honam region increased more than 150-fold, from 260 megawatt-hours in 2023 to 39,527 megawatt-hours in 2025. In response, the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment (MCEE) announced plans to replace hard limits on grid connections with curtailable access and battery storage, aiming to accommodate more than 100 GW of renewable energy capacity by 2030.[41] These measures illustrate the technical and regulatory overhaul required to overcome grid rigidity.

The Finance Gap in Developing Nations

A critical barrier to the global energy transition is the disparity in financial resources between developed and developing nations. While countries like the EU-27 have successfully reduced emissions by 37.3% since 1990 through substantial policy support and investment, developing economies face significant hurdles in mobilizing the capital necessary for large-scale renewable deployment and grid modernization.

China’s experience demonstrates the scale of investment required. To achieve carbon neutrality by 2060, China needs new investment of around 138 trillion yuan (US$20 trillion) between 2020 and 2050 in the energy system alone, representing over 2.5% of its annual GDP.[44] This magnitude of funding necessitates a robust domestic green finance industry and significant attraction of international investors. However, many developing nations lack the institutional framework and creditworthiness to access global capital markets on favorable terms, leading to a reliance on fossil fuels that offer lower upfront costs despite higher long-term environmental and economic risks.

Key Structural Barriers
  • Infrastructure Lock-in: Long-lived fossil fuel assets create economic incentives to continue operations, delaying the shift to renewables.
  • Grid Rigidity: Traditional grids lack the flexibility to handle variable renewable output, resulting in high curtailment rates and wasted energy.
  • Financial Constraints: Developing nations face a massive funding gap for green infrastructure, limiting their ability to transition away from fossil fuels despite abundant renewable resources.
  • Market Design Flaws: Electricity markets often fail to value the flexibility and storage capabilities needed to integrate high shares of variable renewables, leading to cannibalization effects.

Addressing these systemic barriers requires more than incremental policy adjustments. It demands a fundamental restructuring of energy markets, significant investment in grid modernization and storage technologies, and innovative financial mechanisms to bridge the gap between developed and developing economies. Without tackling these structural roots, the divergence between rising total emissions and climate targets will persist, undermining global efforts to limit warming to 1.5°C.

Conclusion and Recommendations

Strategic Imperatives for a Divergent Climate Trajectory

The empirical record of the past three decades reveals a stark divergence in global climate trajectories. While the European Union (EU-27) has successfully decoupled economic activity from carbon emissions, reducing its total CO2 output by 37.3% since 1990, global emissions have surged by 69.8% to reach 38,599 Mt in 2024[4]. This disparity underscores a fundamental structural challenge: the rapid industrialization of emerging economies, particularly China and India, has outpaced the decarbonization efforts of advanced industrial nations. Current policy frameworks are insufficient to align with the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C limit, with United Nations assessments projecting a catastrophic 2.8°C of warming by the end of the century under existing measures[17]. Other analyses estimate this trajectory at approximately 2.7°C, indicating that even optimistic interpretations of current pledges fall drastically short of scientific requirements[45]. Closing this implementation gap requires not merely incremental adjustments but a systemic restructuring of energy markets, grid infrastructure, and international equity mechanisms.

Critical Warning

The window to limit warming to 1.5°C is closing rapidly. Even if all new climate targets submitted in 2025 are fully implemented, global emissions will only decrease by 12% by 2035 compared to 2019 levels, far below the 55% reduction required[17].

Recommendations for Policy Reform

To address the structural barriers identified in this report, policymakers must prioritize three interconnected domains: market mechanism reform, infrastructure modernization, and equitable transition financing. The current reliance on voluntary Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) has proven inadequate. The 2025 NDC synthesis indicates that while 89% of parties now communicate economy-wide targets, the aggregate ambition remains misaligned with physical climate limits[43]. Mandatory, legally binding enforcement mechanisms, such as those pioneered by the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), must be expanded globally to prevent carbon leakage and ensure that decarbonization does not simply shift emissions to jurisdictions with weaker regulations.

Market Reform

Strengthening Carbon Pricing

Expand emissions trading systems (ETS) to cover indirect emissions and lower thresholds. In South Korea, the K-ETS must evolve beyond its current scope to drive deeper industrial decarbonization, addressing the high per-capita emissions of 11.29 tons recorded in 2024.

Infrastructure

Grid Modernization & Storage

Address renewable curtailment through massive investment in transmission capacity and battery storage. South Korea’s curtailment rates increased more than 150-fold from 2023 to 2025, highlighting a critical bottleneck in integrating clean energy.

Case Study Implications: South Korea

South Korea presents a unique paradox in the global transition. Despite being a technological leader, it remains heavily reliant on fossil fuels, with renewables accounting for only 10.4% of electricity generation. This lags significantly behind the EU-27’s 47.7% share and even the global average of 33.8%. The nation’s high per-capita emissions of 11.29 tons reflect an industrial structure that has not yet undergone the same degree of green transformation seen in Europe. To bridge this gap, South Korea must accelerate the deployment of non-fossil fuel sources while simultaneously upgrading its grid infrastructure to handle the intermittency of renewable inputs. The failure to address grid curtailment risks rendering future renewable investments inefficient, as evidenced by the recent spike in wasted clean energy.

Policy Domain Current Status (2025) Recommended Action
Renewable Share Korea: 10.4% Accelerate permitting for wind and solar; mandate storage integration.
Carbon Pricing K-ETS active but limited scope Lower participation thresholds; link with international carbon markets.
Grid Infrastructure Curtailment rising sharply Invest in smart grid technologies and long-duration energy storage.

Implementation Checklist for Policymakers

Audit Grid Capacity: Conduct immediate technical assessments of transmission bottlenecks to reduce renewable curtailment rates.
Revise NDC Targets: Align 2035 emission reduction targets with the 55% cut required to maintain a viable 1.5°C pathway.
Expand Carbon Markets: Integrate industrial sectors currently exempt from emissions trading schemes and implement border carbon adjustments.
Prioritize Equity: Ensure that climate finance reaches emerging economies to support their transition without compromising development goals.
Enforce Accountability: Establish independent monitoring bodies to verify progress against statutory climate obligations rather than voluntary pledges.

The path to a stable climate is no longer a matter of technological feasibility but of political will and structural reform. As the world heads toward a 2.8°C warming trajectory, the cost of inaction far exceeds the investment required for a rapid transition. Policymakers must move beyond incrementalism and embrace the systemic changes necessary to realign global economies with planetary boundaries. The tools exist; the imperative now is their swift and equitable deployment.

Conclusion and Recommendations

Data Basis and Limitations

The quantitative analysis presented in this report is grounded in public datasets and authoritative assessments available as of October 28, 2026. All figures reflect the state of knowledge up to this date; subsequent data releases or policy adjustments occurring after this cutoff are not incorporated. Readers should interpret the findings within the context of these temporal and methodological boundaries. The integrity of the comparative analysis relies on a transparent acknowledgment of how different sources define, measure, and project climate metrics. Discrepancies in scope, period, and modeling assumptions are inherent to global climate data aggregation and must be accounted for when drawing cross-jurisdictional conclusions.

Data Notes

The derived figures are calculated from the reference data. These derived metrics—such as percentage changes and per-capita normalizations—are strictly based on the raw inputs provided in the reference tables. They do not represent independent external audits but rather internal consistency checks applied to the source material.

Temporal and Scope Variability

A primary limitation in synthesizing global climate data lies in the heterogeneity of reporting bases. Sources frequently employ different temporal windows—such as January–May partial years versus full-calendar-year aggregates—or distinct geographic scopes, such as global totals excluding specific regions like China. Consequently, figures presented in this report are explicitly stated with their corresponding period and scope to prevent misinterpretation. Direct comparison between metrics derived from different bases is methodologically unsound without appropriate normalization. For instance, a half-year growth rate cannot be linearly extrapolated to an annual figure without accounting for seasonal variations in energy demand and renewable generation potential.

This variability is particularly evident in the assessment of renewable energy adoption. Global estimates for the share of renewables in electricity generation in 2025 vary across authoritative sources. One assessment places this figure at 33% [13], while another, dated April 21, 2026, reports a share of 33.8% [12]. Both figures are retained in this report to illustrate the range of current estimates. They are not merged into a single average, nor is one silently preferred over the other.

Divergence in Climate Projections

Long-term climate projections are subject to similar uncertainties, driven by differences in economic modeling, policy implementation assumptions, and feedback loop parameters. Estimates of global warming by 2100 under current policy trajectories exhibit notable divergence. One major assessment, published on November 5, 2025, projects a temperature increase of 2.8°C [17]. In contrast, another analysis released two days earlier, on November 3, 2025, estimates a slightly lower trajectory of approximately 2.7°C [45].

These discrepancies do not necessarily indicate error but rather reflect the sensitivity of climate models to varying inputs regarding fossil fuel subsidy phase-outs, deforestation rates, and the speed of clean technology diffusion. This report presents both figures to acknowledge the range of plausible outcomes. The 0.1°C difference, while seemingly small, represents significant variance in cumulative carbon budgets and the associated risk of triggering irreversible tipping points. Policymakers interpreting these projections should consider the upper bound (2.8°C) as a conservative baseline for risk assessment, ensuring that adaptation strategies are robust enough to withstand higher-than-expected warming scenarios.

Implications for Policy Interpretation

The limitations outlined above necessitate a cautious approach to policy benchmarking. When comparing national performance, such as the emission reductions achieved by the EU-27 or the rapid growth in China’s total emissions, it is crucial to recognize that these figures are snapshots of a dynamic system. The reported 37.3% reduction in EU-27 emissions since 1990, for example, is a historical achievement that may not linearly predict future decarbonization rates as the easiest abatement opportunities are exhausted. Similarly, the 394.8% increase in China’s emissions reflects a specific phase of industrialization that may not be replicable in other developing economies due to changing global trade dynamics and technology costs.

Furthermore, the distinction between territorial emissions and consumption-based emissions remains a critical blind spot in many national inventories. While this report primarily relies on territorial data (emissions produced within a country’s borders), this approach can obscure the carbon footprint embedded in imported goods. Countries with high service-based economies may appear to have lower emissions while effectively outsourcing their carbon intensity to manufacturing hubs. This structural disparity is not fully captured in the per-capita metrics presented, which use population denominators but do not adjust for trade-related carbon flows. Future analyses should strive to integrate consumption-based accounting to provide a more equitable basis for international comparison.

In summary, the data presented herein offers a rigorous snapshot of the global climate landscape as of late 2026. It highlights clear trends—such as the decoupling of economic growth from emissions in advanced economies and the persistent rise in absolute global totals—while acknowledging the margins of error in specific metrics. Users of this report are advised to treat the figures as indicative of broad directions rather than precise absolutes, particularly when dealing with forward-looking projections or rapidly evolving sectors like renewable energy deployment. The convergence of multiple sources on the general trajectory of warming and emission growth provides confidence in the overall narrative, even as specific point estimates remain subject to ongoing refinement.
